text:
Every text pipeline starts with one small decision: where does one word end, and the next one begin? Take this sentence. I don't think Mr. Lee's plan will work, but we'll see! The obvious move is to split it at the spaces. That gives eleven pieces. But work still carries its comma, and see its exclamation mark, so neither would ever match the plain word. And the negation in don't is hidden inside a single piece. NLTK's tokenizer, word tokenize, cuts the way a linguist would. Don't splits in two, so the negation becomes a token of its own. Lee's sheds its possessive, we'll its will, and the comma and the exclamation mark stand alone. That's sixteen tokens. And Mr. keeps its period, right where it belongs. Each piece is a token: one meaningful unit of text. Usually a word, but sometimes a number, a symbol, or a punctuation mark. One level up, the period itself gets tricky.

A period can end a sentence. It can also shorten a title, like doctor, or mark a decimal point. Here's a line with all three. Dr. Lee earned two point five million. He smiled. Wasn't that great? Split that at every period, and it falls into five pieces. It breaks after doctor, breaks inside two point five, and never notices the question mark. NLTK's sentence tokenizer, called Punkt, knows about abbreviations and decimals. It returns three clean sentences. And even the right word cuts depend on what you're reading.

Take a tweet, with a hashtag, a handle and a smiley. The default tokenizer breaks all three apart. The hash comes off NLP, the at sign comes off the name, and the smiley falls into a colon and a bracket. NLTK's tweet tokenizer keeps each one whole. Neither one is wrong. The right tokens are the ones that keep the units your task cares about. But even clean tokens can spell one word several ways.
